video_title: MacroVoices #547 Daniel Lacalle: The Future of Reserve Currency
gist: Tressis chief economist Daniel Lacalle argues that developed-market governments (US, Eurozone, Japan, UK, China) have breached the three limits — economic, fiscal, and inflationary — that made their sovereign debt credible as a global reserve asset, and that the displacement of that system will be driven by citizens and investors, not central banks. He and Erik Townsend converge on stablecoins as the practical bridge out of Treasury-centric reserves, read central bank gold buying and the BRICS currency project as backward-looking attempts to preserve centralized fiat control, and contrast the ECB's CBDC push with the Trump administration's ban-CBDC / embrace-crypto strategy to entrench the dollar.

insights.claim: Sovereign debt loses its status as a credible reserve asset when a government breaches three specific limits — the economic limit (debt grows faster than GDP while productivity stagnates), the fiscal limit (higher taxes and stimulus worsen deficits and interest burden), and the inflationary limit (monetary excess spills into consumer prices).
insights.speaker: Daniel Lacalle
insights.so_what: Gives a testable three-part scorecard for ranking sovereign bond markets — screen issuers on debt/GDP growth differential, interest expense as share of budget, and realized inflation, rather than on credit ratings.
insights.quote: Governments have surpassed all of the limits that give them credibility to maintain their debt as a reserve of value. And those limits are the economic limit, the fiscal limit, and the inflationary limit.

insights.claim: The US, Eurozone, Japan, the UK and China have all breached the economic, fiscal and inflationary limits to differing degrees, which paradoxically forces them to cooperate to keep the monetary system stable rather than compete for reserve status.
insights.speaker: Daniel Lacalle
insights.so_what: Argues against the trade of one major sovereign bloc 'winning' at another's expense; relative-value FX trades between majors are choices among deteriorating assets, not directional bets on soundness.

insights.claim: The 2020-2021 inflation surge was the decisive breach of the inflationary limit, and it hit hardest in exactly those economies that had been arguing money supply and debt could expand without inflationary consequences.
insights.speaker: Daniel Lacalle
insights.so_what: Frames the 2020-21 episode as a permanent credibility break, not a transitory shock — implies a structurally higher term premium on long-dated developed-market sovereign debt.

insights.claim: Currency is best understood as an IOU representing the state's credit credibility, and state-issued money is predominantly government debt — so questions about currency debasement and questions about sovereign solvency are the same question.
insights.speaker: Daniel Lacalle
insights.so_what: Links FX and rates analysis into one frame: deteriorating fiscal credibility should show up in currency purchasing power, not only in yields.
insights.quote: currency at the end of the day is an IOU in which the government basically is demonstrating its credit credibility

themes.theme: What Actually Kills a Reserve Currency

insights.claim: The vague phrase 'loss of confidence' in a currency has a concrete, measurable definition: holding that country's long-term debt starts producing losses in real terms and sometimes in nominal terms.
insights.speaker: Daniel Lacalle
insights.so_what: Makes reserve-currency erosion trackable: monitor rolling real total returns on 10y+ sovereign paper as the leading indicator of reserve-manager rotation.
insights.quote: what it means is that holding the long-term debt of these countries is generating losses in real terms and sometimes in nominal terms. That's why you lose confidence in that instrument and with it lose confidence in the currency.

insights.claim: Developed-market sovereign debt functionally replaced gold as the world's reserve asset — meaning the current system is a historically recent construct, not a permanent feature, and the 'lowest risk asset' framing of government bonds is a relatively new idea.
insights.speaker: Daniel Lacalle
insights.so_what: Supports viewing gold's re-entry into reserve portfolios as a reversion to a prior norm rather than an anomaly.

insights.claim: The dollar holds reserve status not because it is good but because the fiat alternatives are worse, and its real underpinnings are independent institutions, open capital markets, and the absence of capital and currency controls.
insights.speaker: Daniel Lacalle
insights.so_what: Identifies the specific policy actions — capital controls, institutional capture — that would genuinely threaten dollar status, as distinct from deficits alone; watch those as the real tail risk.
insights.quote: the dollar is not the world reserve currency in the fiat world because it's better, but because the alternatives are worse

insights.claim: All the major fiat currencies are deteriorating against gold simultaneously, so relative FX strength between majors reflects only which one is degrading more slowly, not good policy.
insights.speaker: Daniel Lacalle
insights.so_what: Argues for measuring currency performance against gold rather than against a fiat basket like DXY — a long-gold-versus-fiat-basket expression rather than a cross-currency bet.
insights.quote: all of them are worsening relative to gold

insights.claim: The euro has lost second place as a reserve asset on central bank balance sheets to gold — a concrete marker of reserve rotation away from developed-market fiat debt.
insights.speaker: Daniel Lacalle
insights.so_what: A hard datapoint supporting structural central-bank gold demand; it also frames ECB behavior as defensive rather than strategic.
insights.quote: the euro has lost the second place as a reserve asset in Central Bank's balance sheets in favor of gold

insights.claim: The ECB's push for a central bank digital currency is a panic response to losing reserve-currency standing — an attempt to impose usage of the euro by digital means rather than to earn it.
insights.speaker: Daniel Lacalle
insights.so_what: Reframes the digital euro as a signal of European monetary weakness rather than innovation — bearish read on euro reserve share and on EU financial-sector regulatory direction.
insights.quote: Many central banks like the European Central Bank are panicking about the risk of losing the role as reserve currency

insights.claim: A CBDC is the structural opposite of a cryptocurrency: it centralizes and makes money confiscable and surveillable, whereas a decentralized crypto asset cannot be confiscated and sits outside the state-issuance system.
insights.speaker: Daniel Lacalle
insights.so_what: Cuts against lumping 'digital money' into one theme — the two are competing designs, and policy that favors one is typically hostile to the other.

insights.claim: The US administration under Trump is banning central bank digital currencies while embracing stablecoins and crypto specifically as a strategy to cement the dollar's reserve role, on the logic that every crypto transaction has a dollar on the other side.
insights.speaker: Daniel Lacalle
insights.so_what: Implies durable US policy support for dollar-backed stablecoin infrastructure and crypto domiciling in the US — a structural tailwind for that industry and for marginal Treasury demand.

insights.claim: The core case against CBDCs is that they hand the central bank a complete record of what citizens consume, invest, spend and owe, arriving precisely as confidence in central bank independence is already eroding.
insights.speaker: Daniel Lacalle
insights.so_what: Predicts strong political resistance to CBDC adoption in democracies — adoption timelines and vendor revenue expectations tied to CBDC rollouts are likely too optimistic.
insights.quote: The Trump administration sees Central Bank digital currencies as surveillance disguised as money and as a tool of state repression.

insights.claim: The functional purpose of a CBDC is to speed up the transmission mechanism of monetary policy by bypassing the commercial banking channel — which, in economies that have already breached the inflationary limit, means a materially higher risk of faster inflation.
insights.speaker: Daniel Lacalle
insights.so_what: If a CBDC is ever adopted, it should be traded as an inflation-regime change and a structural negative for bank deposit franchises, not as a neutral plumbing upgrade.

insights.claim: CBDC experiments implemented globally so far have been an outright failure, albeit mostly in countries where failure was predictable.
insights.speaker: Daniel Lacalle
insights.so_what: Evidence to discount near-term CBDC disruption scenarios and the associated infrastructure spend narrative.
insights.quote: the experiment of Central Bank digital currency so far all over the world has been an absolute disaster

insights.claim: The standard defense of dollar hegemony — that no other market has the depth and liquidity to absorb central-bank-sized flows the way the Treasury market does — is neutralized by stablecoins, because once global transacting migrates to stablecoins the backing asset can be switched without changing the transaction layer.
insights.speaker: Erik Townsend
insights.so_what: The most actionable idea in the episode: dollar-reserve risk should be monitored at the stablecoin-collateral layer, not just in Treasury auction demand — watch for any large stablecoin re-collateralizing away from USD paper.
insights.quote: you're exactly one computer programmer epiphany away from having a viable replacement for the US dollar as the global financial system

insights.claim: Stablecoins are the bridge from the fully centralized monetary system to a decentralized reserve system — solving the transition problem that made reserve-currency change look impossible.
insights.speaker: Daniel Lacalle
insights.so_what: Positions stablecoin rails as strategic infrastructure rather than a payments niche — relevant for issuers, custodians and settlement networks.
insights.quote: stablecoins are the the bridge that takes us from the old to the new

insights.claim: Because the collateral backing stablecoins can be swapped, the existence of stablecoins itself disciplines the US government and Federal Reserve into defending the dollar's purchasing power rather than disguising fiscal imbalances.
insights.speaker: Daniel Lacalle
insights.so_what: Implies a hidden hawkish constraint on US policy that most macro models omit; a bullish tail case for dollar purchasing power discipline.

insights.claim: Regulating stablecoins into being dollar-only is not achievable — that ship has sailed, because regulation is an attempt to re-centralize a system whose value to users comes precisely from decentralization; the only lever left is leading by example as a reserve asset.
insights.speaker: Daniel Lacalle
insights.so_what: Argues that regulatory moats around dollar stablecoins won't hold — non-USD and non-fiat-backed stablecoins should be expected to gain share over time.
insights.quote: that is a ship that is long gone. It's impossible to regulate a system in which the key, the central part that makes it valuable for people is that it is decentralized.

insights.claim: Crypto assets and stablecoins are on track to take over the job central banks abandoned — constraining government excess — because central banks have lost independence and now accommodate rather than limit fiscal imbalances.
insights.speaker: Daniel Lacalle
insights.so_what: Reframes crypto's investment case as a monetary-discipline mechanism rather than a risk asset — implies correlation to fiscal deterioration, not to tech equities.

themes.theme: Gold, BRICS and the Backward-Looking Bloc

insights.claim: Central banks are buying gold rather than digital assets because gold lets them de-dollarize without decentralizing — it strengthens their balance sheet and separates them from a US-centric system while preserving state control over money.
insights.speaker: Daniel Lacalle
insights.so_what: Explains why central bank gold demand can persist for years without any corresponding official crypto adoption — do not treat the two as substitutable flows.
insights.quote: Gold doesn't signify a threat for those central banks and their own domestic currency.

insights.claim: The BRICS currency project is a move backward toward a pre-dollar world of capital controls, currency controls and non-independent institutions, not an embrace of a decentralized monetary future — which is why it is unlikely to produce a credible reserve alternative.
insights.speaker: Daniel Lacalle
insights.so_what: A direct fade of the 'BRICS currency displaces the dollar' narrative; the displacement risk comes from decentralized rails, not from a state-led bloc currency.
insights.quote: the idea of a BRICS crypto Sorry, of a BRICS currency is not an idea of embracing the future, but is an idea of going to the past

insights.claim: Governments encouraging their central banks to swap dollars and euros for gold are simultaneously trying to cling to the fiat system and hold the power of money — a contradiction that limits how far official de-dollarization can actually go.
insights.speaker: Daniel Lacalle
insights.so_what: Sets a ceiling on official-sector de-dollarization: expect reserve diversification into gold but continued resistance to any asset the state cannot control.
insights.quote: you cannot bake the cake and eat it

insights.claim: The transition to decentralized money will be led by individual investors and citizens, not by central banks — every prior monetary revolution was adopted by citizens first, with governments, empires and central banks understanding it last.
insights.speaker: Daniel Lacalle
insights.so_what: Suggests watching retail and corporate adoption metrics — not official-sector reserve allocations — as the leading indicator of monetary regime change.
insights.quote: All monetary revolutions have happened because citizens have embraced them first, and governments, empires, central banks, however you want to call it cuz all they're all same, basically just were the last to understand it.

insights.claim: The base case is coexistence rather than replacement: fiat currencies and independent decentralized currencies will run in parallel, with most governments actively trying to ban or limit the independent ones.
insights.speaker: Daniel Lacalle
insights.so_what: Sets expectations against a binary hyperbitcoinization or dollar-collapse trade; positions for a long grinding regulatory conflict with periodic bans as headline risk.

insights.claim: Currency competition benefits even citizens who never leave state money, because the existence of an exit option limits how far a government can dilute its currency's purchasing power — the Hayek 'Choice in Currency' argument now made operational by technology.
insights.speaker: Daniel Lacalle
insights.so_what: Implies a structural disinflationary constraint emerging from crypto adoption — a variable absent from most inflation models.

insights.claim: Inflation is characterized as deliberately created by governments to dilute future commitments denominated in a currency they themselves issue — making it a policy choice rather than an accident.
insights.speaker: Daniel Lacalle
insights.so_what: Argues persistent above-target inflation should be the base case for any heavily indebted issuer, favoring real assets and inflation-linked exposure over nominal long duration.

insights.claim: Recent trade agreements between the United States, the EU and other partners demonstrate that no bloc can win at any cost and none can decouple from the US as a trading and financial partner, so cooperation is the uncomfortable but inevitable outcome.
insights.speaker: Daniel Lacalle
insights.so_what: Argues against pricing in a full fragmentation scenario for cross-border capital flows despite the trade-war rhetoric.

insights.claim: Trump will shake the foundations of the existing monetary and trade system but is a negotiator who is not looking to destroy it, so expectations of a deliberate US-led demolition of the current order are overstated.
insights.speaker: Daniel Lacalle
insights.so_what: Caps the tail risk on US-driven systemic rupture; volatility around policy headlines is more tradeable than a structural break.
insights.quote: I don't think that President Trump is going to completely annihilate the system as we know it. I think that he is a negotiator and and he's going to shake the foundations, but he's not looking to to destroy them.

insights.claim: Crypto currently poses only limited competitive threat in scale terms — the market cap of Bitcoin and cryptocurrencies is described as exceedingly small relative to the market cap of fiat currencies — yet central banks are already reacting to it.
insights.speaker: Daniel Lacalle
insights.so_what: The policy reaction is running ahead of the actual size of the threat, which means regulatory risk to crypto is front-loaded relative to fundamentals.
